reference.source: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children, and Adolescents
clinicalPearls: Double-orifice mitral valve divides the inflow into two orifices through a fibrous bridge, each often with its own subvalvar apparatus.
Three morphological types are described: complete bridge, incomplete bridge and duplicate or hole type, best defined on short-axis and 3D echocardiography.
It is frequently an incidental finding with normal function but may cause stenosis or regurgitation.
There is a strong association with atrioventricular septal defect and other left-heart lesions such as coarctation and bicuspid aortic valve.
Parasternal short-axis imaging shows two distinct orifices with a double-barrel appearance in diastole.
Surgeons should avoid dividing the bridge to create a single orifice, as this can worsen regurgitation, so repair is tailored to the dominant lesion.
Balloon or surgical intervention is reserved for significant stenosis or regurgitation rather than for the morphology itself.
reference.pathophysiology: A fibrous bridge of tissue divides the mitral orifice into two openings, each usually supported by its own set of chordae and papillary muscle. In the complete bridge type the division extends from annulus to leaflet edge producing two separate orifices; in the incomplete or eccentric type the division is confined to the leaflet margin; and in the duplicate or hole type a small accessory orifice sits within one leaflet. Valve function is often normal, but stenosis can arise when the orifices are small or the subvalvar apparatus is abnormal, and regurgitation can occur through deficient coaptation. The anomaly is strongly associated with atrioventricular septal defect and other left-heart obstructive lesions.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital mitral stenosis from parachute valve or supravalvar ring
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography with parasternal short-axis imaging
Screening for atrioventricular septal defect and left-heart obstruction
redFlags: Severe mitral stenosis with pulmonary hypertension
Severe regurgitation with left ventricular volume overload
Heart failure or failure to thrive
Coexisting significant atrioventricular septal defect or outflow tract obstruction
reference.prognosis: When valve function is normal the anomaly needs no treatment and prognosis is excellent; outcome in symptomatic cases depends on the severity of stenosis or regurgitation and associated defects, with repair being more complex than for a single-orifice valve.
pitfalls: Mistaking the two orifices for vegetations or an intracardiac mass
Surgically dividing the bridge and precipitating severe regurgitation
Missing an associated atrioventricular septal defect
Underestimating stenosis when each individual orifice is small
references: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children, and Adolescents
Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
management: When valve function is normal, which is the usual situation, no intervention is required and the anomaly is simply observed
Reserve surgical repair for haemodynamically significant stenosis or regurgitation, tailoring it to the dominant lesion rather than dividing the fibrous bridge, which risks worsening regurgitation
Treat symptomatic left-heart obstruction or regurgitation with heart-failure measures such as diuretics and afterload reduction, pending or in addition to surgery
Monitor with serial transthoracic and three-dimensional transoesophageal echocardiography and Doppler inflow gradients for progressive stenosis or regurgitation
Actively screen for and manage associated lesions, including atrioventricular septal defect, coarctation and bicuspid aortic valve
Manage under paediatric and congenital cardiology, with congenital cardiac surgical input when intervention is contemplated
